clue.text: Bolt on knave of hearts in a play

parts.note: someone soft of heart, kindly and mild, is gentle
the knave in a pack of cards is also called the jack

explanation.surface: A playwright named Bolt dramatises the Knave of Hearts from the nursery rhyme.
explanation.walkthrough: Robert Bolt, author of A Man for All Seasons, also wrote Gentle Jack (1963); 'Bolt on' tells you whose play it is. The pieces come in reverse clue order: 'of hearts' then 'knave'.
explanation.definitionFit: Gentle Jack is the title of a stage work by the English dramatist Robert Bolt.

clue.text: A way out offered by Cecil Day-Lewis

definitions.meaning: a hinged barrier in a wall or fence through which one leaves
The ... (1962) is a poetry collection by the Poet Laureate C. Day-Lewis

explanation.definitionFit: A gate is an opening for exit, and The Gate is the title of a book of Day-Lewis's verse.

clue.text: Festival doctor in The Suicide Club

definitions.meaning: the Christmas feast, from the French word for it
A character in Robert Louis Stevenson's story sequence The Suicide Club

explanation.definitionFit: Christmas is a festival also known by this French-derived name, which Stevenson gave to a physician in his tales.

clue.text: "But — —-/ Is cat and dog in this double-bed of a world" (Christopher Fry)

definitions.text: "But — —-/ Is cat and dog in this double-bed of a world" (Christopher Fry)

parts.words: "But — —-/ Is cat and dog in this double-bed of a world" (Christopher Fry)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from Fry's verse play The Lady's Not for Burning: the missing pair of opposites quarrel like cat and dog

explanation.surface: A line of verse from Christopher Fry with words missing, about a squabbling couple sharing the world's bed.
explanation.definitionFit: The paired opposites of existence and its ending are the two things Fry pictures fighting like cat and dog.

clue.text: Captain who frequently booked a major

definitions.text: Captain who frequently booked a major

parts.words: Captain who frequently booked a major
parts.note: Captain W. E. ... wrote dozens of books about the flying ace Biggles, who held the rank of Major in the early stories; 'booked' means put into books, not arrested

explanation.surface: A ship's or army captain keeps putting a senior officer on report.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Booked' suggests a disciplinary charge; here it means written into books. Captain W. E. Johns created Biggles, Major Bigglesworth of 266 Squadron.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of the Biggles adventures signed himself Captain W. E. Johns, and his hero was a Major.

clue.text: First woman to follow excellent student in enamel work

parts.note: champ is informal for excellent or first-rate
L is the learner, as on a British learner driver's plate
Eve is the first woman in the Book of Genesis

explanation.surface: A top pupil is succeeded by the first female student on an enamelling course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to follow' puts the woman last. L for student comes from the red L plate a British learner driver must show; 'excellent' is the informal adjective champ, not a noun.
explanation.definitionFit: Champlevé is a technique of enamelling in which hollows cut into metal are filled with vitreous colour.

clue.text: Decisive snakes like an afterthought in play

parts.note: as means like, in a comparison
PS, postscript, is an afterthought added to a letter

explanation.surface: Snakes play a decisive part, almost as an afterthought, in a drama.
explanation.walkthrough: The play is Antony and Cleopatra, where the asps decide Cleopatra's end late in the action; 'in play' points to it.
explanation.definitionFit: Small venomous serpents of Egypt, the kind Cleopatra used to kill herself, settling the tragedy.

clue.text: Propose as a different recent art form

indicators.note: a different arrangement of the letters of the preceding words is called for

explanation.surface: Proposing a different modern medium of artistic expression.
explanation.walkthrough: 'different' rearranges PROPOSE, AS and A together.
explanation.definitionFit: Serial radio and television dramas of domestic life are a twentieth-century popular genre.

clue.text: 'Our church is, I believe, the first — - —church in America' (Peter De Vries)

definitions.text: 'Our church is, I believe, the first — - —church in America' (Peter De Vries)

parts.words: 'Our church is, I believe, the first — - —church in America' (Peter De Vries)
parts.note: a fill-in-the-blank quotation from De Vries's comic novel The Mackerel Plaza: the missing compound describes a building on staggered floors, as of a suburban house

explanation.surface: A quotation from a comic American novelist about a pioneering church building.
explanation.definitionFit: A building design with floors at staggered heights, typical of suburban houses, which De Vries applies to a church.

clue.text: Epiphany closely preceding play

definitions.meaning: the Christian feast on 6 January, the twelfth after Christmas
the day comes just after the eve that gives Shakespeare's comedy Twelfth Night its title

explanation.definitionFit: The feast of the Magi falls on the twelfth day of Christmas, hard by the night named in Shakespeare's comedy title.

clue.text: Bellow recalling mad king

definitions.meaning: ... Bellow, the American novelist, gives his first name
the first king of Israel, who fell into fits of madness

explanation.walkthrough: 'Bellow' looks like a verb meaning shout, but it is the novelist's surname.
explanation.definitionFit: The forename of the author of Herzog is also that of the Old Testament king tormented by an evil spirit.

clue.text: Shelley's doctor

parts.note: Mary Shelley's novel features a scientist, Victor, who makes a creature; not Percy Shelley, and not a physician

explanation.definitionFit: Victor, the creator of the monster in Mary Shelley's 1818 novel, is often loosely called a doctor.

clue.text: Verne's adhesive servant

parts.note: Phileas Fogg's French valet in Around the World in Eighty Days shares his name with a gummed tape used to bind picture frames

explanation.surface: A servant in a Jules Verne novel who sticks close to his master.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adhesive' seems to describe a clinging valet, but it points to the gummed framing tape of the same name.
explanation.definitionFit: Fogg's valet is named after a master key, and the same word names a framing tape.

clue.text: He laid his heart bare in autobiography

definitions.text: He laid his heart bare in autobiography

parts.words: He laid his heart bare in autobiography
parts.note: refers to the French poet's journal Mon coeur mis à nu, My Heart Laid Bare

explanation.surface: A writer who poured out his innermost feelings in a memoir.
explanation.definitionFit: The author of Les Fleurs du mal left intimate journals titled My Heart Laid Bare.

clue.text: Exultant, like Hayley's music

definitions.meaning: William Hayley, the 18th-century poet, wrote The Triumphs of Music

explanation.definitionFit: Exultant means jubilant after victory, and Hayley's poem celebrates the triumphs of music.

clue.text: Suitable definition for Warner

parts.note: Rex Warner's 1941 novel is titled The ..., so the word fits as a label for him

explanation.surface: Finding an apt dictionary entry for someone called Warner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Aerodrome is the best-known novel by the English writer Rex Warner.

clue.text: Compton Mackenzie's idea of where we live

parts.words: Compton Mackenzie's idea of where we live

explanation.surface: A novelist imagines our home neighbourhood.
explanation.definitionFit: Mackenzie's title names the road that belongs to us, that is, where we live.

clue.text: Sweet as Wilder's Irma, to be seen in Sardou centenary celebration

indicators.note: the letters can be seen running inside the words that follow

explanation.surface: Billy Wilder's charming heroine appears at a festival marking the playwright Sardou's hundredth anniversary.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be seen in' signals letters inside SARDOU CENTENARY; 'celebration' is padding for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Billy Wilder's film Irma la Douce names a heroine called sweet in French; the word also means sweet or gentle in Scots.

clue.text: New Reeve Tale to promote again

explanation.surface: A fresh edition of a Chaucer story, The Reeve's Tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New' rearranges REEVE and TALE; The Reeve's Tale is one of Chaucer's Canterbury Tales.

clue.text: Conspire in novel construction

clue.text: The terrible Eisenstein classic

parts.note: Sergei Eisenstein's film is about the first tsar of Russia, nicknamed the Terrible

explanation.surface: A dreadful film by the Soviet director Eisenstein.
explanation.walkthrough: 'terrible' seems to judge the film, but it is the tsar's epithet.
explanation.definitionFit: Eisenstein's two-part film is named after the 16th-century tsar called the Terrible.
